ety.text: Inherited from Middle English dogge (akin to Scots dug), from Old English dogga, docga, of uncertain origin. The original meaning seems to have been a common dog, as opposed to a well-bred one, or something like 'cur', and perhaps later came to be used for stocky dogs. Possibly a pet-form diminutive with suffix -ga (compare frocga (“frog”), *picga (“pig”)), appended to a base *dog-, *doc- of unclear origin and meaning. One possibility is Old English dox (“dark, swarthy”) (compare frocga from frox).

senses.d: The species Canis familiaris (sometimes designated Canis lupus familiaris), domesticated for thousands of years and of highly variable appearance because of human breeding.
ex: The dog barked all night long.

senses.d: Any member of the family Canidae, including domestic dogs, wolves, coyotes, jackals, and their relatives (extant and extinct).
A male dog, wolf, or fox, as opposed to a bitch or vixen.
The meat of this animal, eaten as food.
ex: Did you know that they eat dog in parts of Asia?

senses.d: A dull, unattractive girl or woman.
Someone who overeats or eats rapidly and noisily.
Someone who is cowardly, worthless, or morally reprehensible.
ex: Come back and fight, you dogs!
DJ Paul is a dog; one you do not trust.

senses.d: Any of various mechanical devices for holding, gripping, or fastening something, particularly with a tooth-like projection.
ex: Whenever possible, let the tree support the weight of the chainsaw. Pivot the saw, using the saw's dogs (spikes) as a fulcrum.

senses.d: To pursue with the intent to catch.
To follow in an annoying or harassing way.
ex: The woman cursed him so that trouble would dog his every step.
But this is not an Athletic that ever looks comfortable at the back – a criticism that has often dogged Marcelo Bielsa's sides.
It is very important to dog down these hatches.

senses.d: To watch, or participate, in sexual activity in a public place.
ex: I admit that I like to dog at my local country park.

senses.d: To intentionally restrict one's productivity as employee; to work at the slowest rate that goes unpunished.
ex: A surprise inspection of the night shift found that some workers were dogging it.

senses.d: To divide (a watch) with a comrade.
ex: Meanwhile, we dogged the watch sections so that both halves of the crew could fetch full sea bags of uniforms and gear […]
Oh man, this game is absolutely dog!

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French chien, from Old French chien, from Latin canis, canem (“dog”). See cognates in regional languages in France : Bourguignon chein, Catalan ca, Corsican cane, cani, Franco-Provençal shin, tsin, Gallo chien, cun, qhun Norman quien, tchian, Occitan can, chin, Picard quien, tchien.
From the Latin canis, canem (“dog”). Cognate with Sicilian cani.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish perro (“cur”) (ca. 1200), of uncertain origin. Originally had a pejorative connotation, but soon began to supplant the Latin word can. Perhaps from a call used for dogs; compare Galician apurrar (“set the dogs on”). Another theory derives it from Iberian; compare Asturian perru.
Inherited from Latin canis, canem (“dog”). Cognate with Catalan ca, Galician can, Portuguese cão.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese can, from Latin canis, canem. Compare Galician and Spanish can.
Uncertain. Likely inherited from Vulgar Latin *cattulus, from Latin catulus, plus the suffix -orro; whence also Spanish cachorro.
